profiles.name: Joseph W. Scherrer
profiles.description: Joseph W. Scherrer was arrested with the Denver Smith Act defendants on August 1, 1954 and released on $5,000 bail. A jury convicted the group on May 25, 1955, but an appellate court ordered a new trial after the Supreme Court’s Yates decision. A second conviction was also reversed in 1961 because prosecutors withheld hundreds of documents. Scherrer remained free on bail while the litigation continued; no service of a prison sentence has been established.

profiles.description: Karley Larsen was an International Woodworkers of America vice-president and Progressive Party figure. Federal agents arrested him at a union convention in Portland on September 17, 1952 and transported him to Seattle in handcuffs and leg irons for prosecution under the Smith Act. After the lengthy Seattle trial, the jury acquitted Larsen in October 1953. The reviewed record does not establish the date on which he obtained release after his arrest.

Federal agents arrested her on August 2, 1954, as one of seven Colorado defendants charged under the Smith Act. She was held in the Denver County Jail until posting $5,000 bail. The defendants were convicted, but years of appeals and retrials followed after the Supreme Court narrowed Smith Act prosecutions. Scherrer remained free on bail after a 1959 sentence of two and a half years, and the Tenth Circuit reversed the convictions again in 1961.

profiles.name: Michael Russo
profiles.description: Michael A. Russo was one of the Massachusetts "Bay State Reds" — the Communist Party members arrested in 1956 and prosecuted under the Smith Act for conspiracy to advocate the overthrow of the U.S. government. He was photographed with his fellow defendants — Otis Archer Hood, Anne Burlak Timpson, Daniel Boone Schirmer, Sidney Lipshires, Geoffrey Warner White, and Edward Strong — after they won their case in 1957, when the prosecution was dismissed in the wake of the Supreme Court's Yates decision. Beyond his role as a Massachusetts Smith Act defendant, the individual record of his life is thinly documented.

An appeals court ordered a new trial in 1958, and the government abandoned the prosecution.

profiles.name: Otis Hood
profiles.description: Otis Archer Hood was the chairman of the Massachusetts Communist Party and the lead figure among the "Bay State Reds" prosecuted in the McCarthy era. In 1954 he was among Communists arrested for violating Massachusetts's state ban on the Communist Party, winning acquittal, and he was acquitted again after a 1956 state indictment for inciting the overthrow of the government. He was then indicted with his comrades under the federal Smith Act for conspiracy to advocate the government's overthrow — charges that were dismissed in 1957 after the Supreme Court's Yates decision. Hood spent decades as a Communist and labor organizer in Massachusetts; his papers are held at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

profiles.name: Sidney Lipshires
profiles.description: Sidney Lipshires was a Communist Party member who joined the Communist Party in 1939 and in 1947 ran for city alderman in Springfield, Massachusetts on the Communist ticket. On May 29, 1956 — the day his daughter was born — he was arrested under the Smith Act for his Communist Party activities, and he went on to serve as executive secretary of the Massachusetts Smith Act Defendants Committee, publishing a pamphlet exposing the law and the tactics used against the accused. The case never reached trial: the Smith Act prosecution collapsed after the Supreme Court's 1957 Yates decision. Lipshires later left the Party, remained active in organized labor, earned a Ph.D., and taught history at Manchester Community College in Connecticut for some thirty years.
